learn_allergies_meta_desc: Plain-language basics on food allergies, cross-contact, label reading, and safer home cooking — informational only, not medical advice.
learn_allergies_disclaimer_body: This page is for general information only. It is not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. If you or someone you care for has a food allergy — especially a severe one — talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your plan. Whip It Flip It does not guarantee that any recipe or feature is free of allergens; always verify ingredients, brands, and preparation for your own situation.
learn_allergies_intro: Short guides to help you think about allergies in the kitchen and at the store. Tap a topic to jump ahead.
learn_section_what_is_body: A food allergy happens when the immune system treats a specific food protein as harmful and reacts to it. Reactions can range from mild symptoms to a severe, whole-body response (anaphylaxis) that needs emergency care. A food intolerance (for example, trouble digesting lactose) is different: it does not involve the same immune mechanism and is managed differently. If you are unsure what you have, a clinician can help you sort it out.
learn_section_common_body: In many countries, certain foods must be called out on packaged labels because they account for most serious reactions. In the United States, the FDA recognizes nine major allergens (often called the "Big 9"): milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, sesame, and soybeans. Other regions use slightly different lists. Your app allergy settings are a helpful filter, but they are not a substitute for checking every product and recipe yourself.
learn_section_cross_body: Cross-contact means an allergen gets into a food by accident — shared cutting boards, knives, fryer oil, toasters, sponges, or hands. Even a small amount can matter for some people. At home, use separate tools and surfaces when needed, clean thoroughly, and be cautious with shared condiments (for example, butter or jam that touched bread). When eating out, ask how food is prepared; staff may not list every risk on a menu.
learn_section_labels_body: Always read the full ingredient list every time you buy a product — recipes change. Look for the allergen statement required in your country (for example, a "Contains:" line in the U.S.). Phrases like "may contain" or "made in a facility with" are voluntary warnings; they mean different things on different products, so follow the guidance your clinician gives you. For unpackaged food (bakery items, bulk bins, deli), ingredient information may be incomplete — ask before you buy or serve.
learn_section_cooking_body: Plan ahead: know who at the table has which allergies, and avoid "hidden" sources (sauces, spice mixes, stocks). Label leftovers with date and major allergens if you share a fridge. Wash hands with soap and water before and after handling allergens. When in doubt, choose a simpler recipe with fewer processed ingredients so you can see everything that goes in. This app can suggest dishes, but you remain responsible for checking each ingredient against your medical needs.
